name: Win16
title: Programming Windows 3.x
intro: Windows 3.0 and 3.1 programs were usually written in C against the 16-bit Windows API. Everything happens through messages: Windows tells your program that a key was pressed, the window needs painting or the user wants to quit, and your code reacts. The same model still sits under modern Windows, so this is also a tour of how Win32 works. To build Win16 code today you need an old compiler such as Borland C++ 3.1, Microsoft C/C++ 7 or Open Watcom, run under Windows 3.1 in an emulator like 86Box, DOSBox-X or Bochs.

lessons.title: WinMain and the message loop
lessons.summary: Register a class, create a window, pump messages.

sections.p: A Windows program starts in WinMain, not main. It registers a window class (which says which function handles its messages), creates a window of that class, and then loops, fetching messages and handing them on.

hPrevInstance is a Win16 detail: if another copy of the program is already running, its class is already registered, so only the first copy registers it (on Win32 this is always NULL). GetMessage waits for the next message and returns 0 when it gets WM_QUIT, which ends the loop. TranslateMessage turns key presses into character messages, and DispatchMessage calls your window procedure.

Windows 3.x programs share the CPU by taking turns: another program can only run while yours is waiting inside GetMessage. A long loop that never returns to the message loop freezes the whole desktop, not just your window.

practice.q: When does the message loop end?
practice.why: GetMessage returns 0 for WM_QUIT, and the while loop stops.

practice.q: What tells Windows which function handles a window's messages?
practice.why: Every window of a registered class sends its messages to that class's window procedure.

practice.q: Why check hPrevInstance in Win16?
practice.why: In Win16, instances of one program share registered classes.
options: Only the first running copy needs to register the class
practice.answer: Only the first running copy needs to register the class

practice.q: A Win16 program runs a 10-second loop without checking messages. What happens?
practice.why: Windows 3.x multitasking is cooperative: no other program runs until yours yields.

practice.q: What does TranslateMessage do in the message loop?
practice.why: TranslateMessage converts virtual-key presses into character messages before DispatchMessage.

practice.q: Where does a Windows program start instead of main?
practice.why: Windows looks for WinMain as the entry point of a GUI program.

sections.p: The window procedure is a big switch on the message number. Handle what you care about and pass everything else to DefWindowProc, which gives standard behaviour such as moving, resizing and closing.

WM_CREATE arrives once when the window is made. WM_PAINT arrives whenever part of the window must be redrawn, so all drawing belongs there, between BeginPaint and EndPaint. WM_DESTROY means the window is going away; posting WM_QUIT with PostQuitMessage ends the message loop. wParam and lParam carry extra details, such as which key was pressed or where the mouse was.

practice.q: Where should a program draw its window's contents?
practice.why: Windows asks for repainting whenever the window is uncovered or resized, so drawing must happen on each WM_PAINT.
options: In WM_PAINT, between BeginPaint and EndPaint
practice.answer: In WM_PAINT, between BeginPaint and EndPaint

practice.q: What should WM_DESTROY usually do in a main window?
practice.why: That posts WM_QUIT, which ends the message loop and the program.

practice.q: What happens to messages your switch does not handle?
practice.why: DefWindowProc supplies the standard behaviour; returning 0 for everything would break moving, sizing and closing.

practice.q: Which message arrives once when the window is first made?
practice.why: WM_CREATE is sent during CreateWindow, before the window is shown.

practice.q: What does BeginPaint return for use while drawing?
practice.why: BeginPaint prepares the window for painting and gives you the HDC to draw with.

lessons.title: Keyboard and mouse
lessons.summary: WM_CHAR, WM_KEYDOWN, mouse positions and asking for a repaint.

sections.p: Input arrives as messages. WM_KEYDOWN reports a key by its virtual-key code (VK_LEFT, VK_F1), which is right for arrows and function keys. WM_CHAR, made by TranslateMessage, reports the character typed, which is right for text. Mouse messages such as WM_LBUTTONDOWN pack the position into lParam: x in the low word, y in the high word.

The handlers above do not draw. They change the program's state and call InvalidateRect, which marks the window as needing a repaint; Windows then sends WM_PAINT when the queue is quiet. Keeping all drawing in one place means the window always looks right, even after another window has covered it.
The window procedure is called afresh for every message, so ordinary local variables forget their values between calls. static locals (or globals) keep state from one message to the next.

practice.q: Which message is best for reading typed text?
practice.why: WM_CHAR gives the actual character, with Shift and keyboard layout already applied.

practice.q: Where is the mouse x position in WM_LBUTTONDOWN?
practice.why: lParam packs x in its low word and y in its high word.

practice.q: What does InvalidateRect(hwnd, NULL, TRUE) do?
practice.why: It marks the area as invalid; Windows later sends WM_PAINT to redraw it.
options: Asks for the whole window to be repainted soon
practice.answer: Asks for the whole window to be repainted soon

practice.q: Why are the position variables static?
practice.why: Each message is a new call to the window procedure; static keeps the values.
options: Ordinary locals are lost between messages
So other programs can read them
practice.answer: Ordinary locals are lost between messages

practice.q: Which message is best for arrow keys such as VK_LEFT?
practice.why: Arrow and function keys arrive as virtual-key codes in WM_KEYDOWN, not as characters.

practice.q: Where is the mouse y position in WM_LBUTTONDOWN?
practice.why: lParam packs x low and y high.

lessons.title: Drawing with the GDI
lessons.summary: Device contexts, pens, brushes and shapes.

sections.p: The GDI (Graphics Device Interface) draws through a device context, the HDC that BeginPaint hands you. To draw in a colour, create a pen (for lines) or a brush (for fills), select it into the DC, draw, then select the old one back and delete yours.

GDI objects come from a small shared pool in Windows 3.x (the GDI heap is 64 KB for the whole system). A program that creates a pen on every paint and never deletes it slowly starves every other program, and the desktop starts drawing wrongly. You must not delete an object while it is still selected into a DC, which is why the old ones are put back first.

Win16 has MoveTo(hdc, x, y), which returns the old position packed into a DWORD. Win32 replaced it with MoveToEx(hdc, x, y, NULL), because 32-bit coordinates no longer fit two to a DWORD. Coordinates in Win16 are 16-bit, from −32768 to 32767.

practice.q: What must happen before DeleteObject(hPen)?
practice.why: An object still selected into a DC must not be deleted.
options: Select the old pen back into the DC
practice.answer: Select the old pen back into the DC

practice.q: Which object fills the inside of a Rectangle?
practice.why: Pens draw outlines and lines; brushes fill areas.

practice.q: What replaced MoveTo in Win32?
practice.why: MoveTo returned two 16-bit coordinates packed in a DWORD, which does not work with 32-bit coordinates.

practice.q: A program creates a brush on every WM_PAINT and never deletes it. What happens over time?
practice.why: In Windows 3.x the GDI heap is shared by every program, so leaks hurt everyone.
options: The shared GDI heap fills and other programs draw wrongly
practice.answer: The shared GDI heap fills and other programs draw wrongly

practice.q: What does CreatePen create?
practice.why: Pens stroke paths; CreateSolidBrush makes a fill colour.
options: A pen for drawing lines and outlines
practice.answer: A pen for drawing lines and outlines

practice.q: What does GetClientRect fill in?
practice.why: GetClientRect returns the client rectangle in a RECT, used for layout and drawing.
options: The size of the window's inside area
practice.answer: The size of the window's inside area

lessons.title: Menus, resources and WM_COMMAND
lessons.summary: The .rc file, menu IDs and handling commands.

sections.p: Menus, dialog layouts, icons and strings live in a resource script (.rc), compiled by the resource compiler and attached to the .exe. Each menu item has an ID number, usually named in a shared header.
sections.code:
/* nutshell.h */
#define IDM_NEW    100
#define IDM_ABOUT  101
#define IDM_EXIT   102

/* nutshell.rc */
#include <windows.h>
#include "nutshell.h"

NutshellMenu MENU
BEGIN
    POPUP "&File"
    BEGIN
        MENUITEM "&New",       IDM_NEW
        MENUITEM SEPARATOR
        MENUITEM "E&xit",      IDM_EXIT
    END
    POPUP "&Help"
    BEGIN
        MENUITEM "&About...",  IDM_ABOUT
    END
END

sections.p: Name the menu in the window class (wc.lpszMenuName = "NutshellMenu";). Choosing an item sends WM_COMMAND with the item's ID in wParam. The & marks the underlined letter for keyboard use.

A Win16 program also needs a .def file. It names the program, says how its code and data segments behave in memory, sets the heap and stack sizes, and exports every function that Windows calls back, such as the window procedure.
sections.code:
NAME         NUTSHELL
DESCRIPTION  'Nutshell for Windows 3.1'
EXETYPE      WINDOWS
STUB         'WINSTUB.EXE'
CODE         PRELOAD MOVEABLE DISCARDABLE
DATA         PRELOAD MOVEABLE MULTIPLE
HEAPSIZE     1024
STACKSIZE    8192
EXPORTS      WndProc

sections.p: WINSTUB.EXE is a tiny DOS program built into the front of every Windows .exe. Run the program from plain DOS and the stub prints “This program requires Microsoft Windows.” instead of crashing.

practice.q: Which message does choosing a menu item send?
practice.why: Menu choices and control notifications both arrive as WM_COMMAND.

practice.q: In Win16, where is the menu item's ID?
practice.why: In Win16, wParam holds the ID of the menu item or control.

practice.q: Why list WndProc under EXPORTS?
practice.why: Win16 callbacks must be exported so Windows can set up the program's data segment when it calls them.
options: Windows calls it from outside the program
To make it public to other programs
So it appears in the menu
practice.answer: Windows calls it from outside the program

practice.q: What does the & in "E&xit" do?
practice.why: The letter after & is underlined and can be pressed with Alt or while the menu is open.
options: Underlines x as the keyboard shortcut
practice.answer: Underlines x as the keyboard shortcut

practice.q: Where do menus and dialog layouts live before they are built into the .exe?
practice.why: The resource compiler turns the .rc into resources attached to the executable.

practice.q: What does WINSTUB.EXE do?
practice.why: The stub is a tiny DOS program at the front of the .exe that refuses to run without Windows.
options: Prints a message if the program is run from plain DOS
practice.answer: Prints a message if the program is run from plain DOS

lessons.title: Dialog boxes and controls
lessons.summary: Dialog templates, dialog procedures, MakeProcInstance and child controls.

sections.p: A dialog box is laid out in the .rc file and driven by a dialog procedure, which looks like a window procedure but returns TRUE for messages it handled and FALSE otherwise. WM_INITDIALOG arrives before it is shown; EndDialog closes it.
sections.code:
AboutBox DIALOG 20, 20, 160, 70
STYLE DS_MODALFRAME | WS_POPUP | WS_CAPTION | WS_SYSMENU
CAPTION "About Nutshell"
BEGIN
    CTEXT         "Nutshell 1.0", -1, 0, 12, 160, 8
    CTEXT         "Gathers nuts since 1992", -1, 0, 24, 160, 8
    DEFPUSHBUTTON "OK", IDOK, 64, 48, 32, 14
END

sections.p: In Win16 a callback such as a dialog procedure cannot be passed straight to Windows. MakeProcInstance builds a small piece of code (a thunk) that loads the right data segment for this copy of the program and then jumps to your function. Free it again with FreeProcInstance. The dialog procedure must also be exported in the .def file.

Buttons, edit boxes and list boxes are child windows of predefined classes such as "BUTTON" and "EDIT". They tell their parent about events with WM_COMMAND. In Win16 the control's ID is in wParam, its window handle in LOWORD(lParam) and the notification code (such as BN_CLICKED) in HIWORD(lParam). Win32 moved the notification code into HIWORD(wParam), one of the classic porting traps.

practice.q: What should a dialog procedure return for a message it did not handle?
practice.why: Dialog procedures return TRUE or FALSE; the dialog manager does the default work when you return FALSE.

practice.q: Why does Win16 code call MakeProcInstance?
practice.why: Several running copies share code but each has its own data segment; the thunk loads the right one.
options: To make a thunk that sets up the data segment before the callback runs
To create a new instance of the program
practice.answer: To make a thunk that sets up the data segment before the callback runs

practice.q: In Win16 WM_COMMAND from a button, where is BN_CLICKED?
practice.why: Win16 puts the notification code in the high word of lParam; Win32 moved it to HIWORD(wParam).

practice.q: Which message lets a dialog fill in its controls before it appears?
practice.why: Dialogs get WM_INITDIALOG after their controls exist but before they are shown.

practice.q: What closes a modal dialog started with DialogBox?
practice.why: EndDialog ends the dialog's own message loop and returns from DialogBox.

practice.q: After DialogBox returns, what should you do with the MakeProcInstance result?
practice.why: The thunk is no longer needed; FreeProcInstance releases it.

lessons.title: Segments and memory
lessons.summary: 16-bit ints, near and far pointers, and moveable global memory.

sections.p: Win16 runs on the 8086 family's segmented memory: an address is a 16-bit segment plus a 16-bit offset, and one segment holds at most 64 KB. A NEAR pointer is just an offset inside the current data segment (2 bytes); a FAR pointer carries a segment too (4 bytes). Win16 API calls that take strings or buffers use far pointers such as LPSTR.
sections.code:
int      n;          /* 16 bits: -32768 to 32767 */
long     big;        /* 32 bits */
char NEAR *pn;       /* 2-byte pointer within our data segment */
char FAR  *pf;       /* 4-byte segment:offset pointer */
LPSTR    text;       /* the same as char FAR * */

sections.p: Large or long-lived blocks come from the global heap. GlobalAlloc returns a handle, not an address, because Windows may move the block to make room. GlobalLock pins it and gives a far pointer; GlobalUnlock lets it move again. Keep blocks unlocked between messages so Windows can shuffle memory.

Windows 3.x might run in real mode (3.0), standard mode or 386 enhanced mode, often on machines with 1 or 2 MB of RAM. Moveable and discardable memory let it compact the heap and throw away code segments it can load again from disk. Handles are what made that possible, and they are why so much of the API passes HWND, HDC, HGLOBAL rather than pointers.
The C library's sprintf works, but Windows has its own smaller wsprintf that writes into a far buffer. TextOut needs the length, which lstrlen gives.

practice.q: How big is an int in a Win16 C compiler?
practice.why: Win16 compilers target 16-bit processors, so int runs from −32768 to 32767; use long for bigger numbers.

practice.q: Why does GlobalAlloc return a handle rather than a pointer?
practice.why: Moveable memory is pinned with GlobalLock only while you use it.
options: Windows may move the block, so its address can change
Pointers are not allowed in C
practice.answer: Windows may move the block, so its address can change

practice.q: What is a FAR pointer?
practice.why: A far pointer can reach any segment; a near one only the current data segment.
options: A segment plus an offset: 4 bytes
An offset in the current segment: 2 bytes
A pointer to the end of memory
practice.answer: A segment plus an offset: 4 bytes

practice.q: What is the most one segment can hold?
practice.why: A 16-bit offset reaches 65,536 bytes.

practice.q: What does GlobalLock do?
practice.why: While locked, Windows will not move the block; unlock it when you are done using the pointer.
options: Pins a moveable block and returns a far pointer
practice.answer: Pins a moveable block and returns a far pointer

practice.q: What is LPSTR?
practice.why: Win16 API string parameters use far pointers so they can reach any segment.
options: char FAR * — a far pointer to a string
A near pointer to an int
practice.answer: char FAR * — a far pointer to a string

lessons.title: Timers and animation
lessons.summary: SetTimer, WM_TIMER, KillTimer and staying cooperative.

sections.p: A program cannot sit in a loop waiting for time to pass: that would freeze Windows 3.x. Instead it asks for WM_TIMER messages with SetTimer and does a little work each time one arrives. Timers are a shared, limited resource, so check that SetTimer succeeded and kill the timer when the window goes away.

WM_TIMER is a low-priority message: it is only delivered when the queue has nothing else, and several missed ticks arrive as one. The PC clock also ticks only about 18.2 times a second, so intervals shorter than about 55 ms are not honoured. For a clock, read the actual time on each tick instead of counting ticks.
For a long calculation, either split it into small steps done on each WM_TIMER, or call PeekMessage now and then inside the loop to let other programs run. Both keep the desktop alive.

practice.q: How should a Win16 program do something every second?
practice.why: Loops and sleeping block cooperative multitasking; Windows 3.x has no threads.
options: A while loop that checks the clock

practice.q: Ten ticks were due while the program was busy. How many WM_TIMER messages arrive?
practice.why: Timer messages are not queued up; missed ticks are combined.

practice.q: Why call KillTimer in WM_DESTROY?
practice.why: A timer that is never killed keeps one of the few system-wide slots busy.
options: Timers are a shared, limited resource
Otherwise the window will not close
To stop the clock for every program
practice.answer: Timers are a shared, limited resource

practice.q: What should you do if SetTimer fails in WM_CREATE?
practice.why: Returning -1 from WM_CREATE cancels window creation when a needed timer cannot be allocated.
options: Return -1 so the window is not created
practice.answer: Return -1 so the window is not created

practice.q: How can a long calculation stay cooperative without SetTimer?
practice.why: PeekMessage lets other programs run while you keep working through a long job.
options: Call PeekMessage now and then inside the loop
practice.answer: Call PeekMessage now and then inside the loop

lessons.title: From Win16 to Win32
lessons.summary: What changed on the way to Windows 95 and NT.

sections.p: Most of the API kept its name when Windows went 32-bit, so a lot of Win16 code compiles for Win32 after a tidy-up. The things that bite are the ones that depended on 16-bit sizes and segments.

int and WPARAM grew to 32 bits, so WM_COMMAND's fields moved: the control ID is now LOWORD(wParam), the notification HIWORD(wParam) and the control handle lParam. NEAR and FAR mean nothing in the flat 32-bit address space. MakeProcInstance is no longer needed. hPrevInstance is always NULL, because every program runs in its own address space. Functions that packed two coordinates into one return value gained Ex versions (MoveToEx, SetWindowOrgEx).

Win32 programs are pre-empted: a long loop freezes only their own window. But a window that stops reading messages still looks hung to the user, so the habits from Win16 (short handlers, timers for slow work) are still good ones. Win32 adds threads for work that really must run for a long time.

practice.q: In Win32 WM_COMMAND, where is the control ID?
practice.why: With a 32-bit wParam, the ID and notification code share it: ID low, code high.

practice.q: What is hPrevInstance in a Win32 program?
practice.why: Each Win32 process has its own address space, so it cannot share another's instance.

practice.q: Which Win16 call is simply unnecessary in Win32?
practice.why: There are no per-instance data segments to set up in a flat address space.

practice.q: Why did MoveTo become MoveToEx?
practice.why: With 32-bit coordinates the old position no longer fits, so MoveToEx returns it through a POINT pointer.
options: The old return value packed two 16-bit coordinates into 32 bits
practice.answer: The old return value packed two 16-bit coordinates into 32 bits

practice.q: In Win32 WM_COMMAND, where is the notification code such as BN_CLICKED?
practice.why: Win32 packs ID and notification into wParam; the control handle is lParam.

practice.q: What happened to NEAR and FAR in Win32?
practice.why: Win32 uses a single linear address space, so segment:offset pointers go away.
options: They mean nothing in the flat 32-bit address space
practice.answer: They mean nothing in the flat 32-bit address space

lessons.title: The clipboard
lessons.summary: Share text between programs with OpenClipboard and CF_TEXT.

sections.p: Windows 3.x programs share selected text (and later bitmaps and other formats) through the clipboard. Only one program owns it at a time. You open it, optionally empty it, put data in or take data out, then close it. The data lives in a global memory block with a format tag such as CF_TEXT.
Check that the format you want is available, then lock the handle Windows gives you. Do not free clipboard data while it is on the clipboard — Windows owns it after a successful SetClipboardData.

After SetClipboardData, do not GlobalFree that handle: the clipboard will free it when something else empties the clipboard. Other common formats include CF_BITMAP and CF_METAFILE. Programs can register private formats with RegisterClipboardFormat when they need a custom structure.

Hold the clipboard open only for the few lines that empty, set or get data. Another program cannot open it while yours holds it, and a crash with the clipboard open can leave the desktop awkward until restart. Copy into your own buffer, close, then work with the copy.

practice.q: What must you call before SetClipboardData?
practice.why: The clipboard is a shared resource; OpenClipboard claims it for your window.

practice.q: Who owns the memory after a successful SetClipboardData?
practice.why: Do not GlobalFree that handle yourself; EmptyClipboard or a later Set will free it.

practice.q: Which format is plain null-terminated text?
practice.why: CF_TEXT is the classic ANSI text format on Win16.

practice.q: What should you do if OpenClipboard fails after GlobalAlloc for a copy?
practice.why: Ownership never passed to the clipboard, so your program must free the allocation.

practice.q: Why keep OpenClipboard … CloseClipboard as short as possible?
practice.why: The clipboard is exclusive; a long hold blocks paste and copy elsewhere.
options: Other programs cannot open the clipboard while you hold it
practice.answer: Other programs cannot open the clipboard while you hold it

practice.q: Before GetClipboardData for text, what is a good check?
practice.why: Avoid opening and finding nothing useful when the user has only a bitmap on the clipboard.

lessons.title: Module definition and DLLs
lessons.summary: The .DEF file, EXPORTS, and a tiny Win16 DLL.

sections.p: A Win16 program is a module. Besides the .C sources you usually ship a .DEF file that names the module, says it is a Windows app, and lists functions that other modules may call. The linker reads that file when it builds the .EXE or .DLL.
sections.code:
; nutshell.def — for an ordinary Windows program
NAME        NUTSHELL
DESCRIPTION 'Gather nuts under Windows 3.1'
EXETYPE     WINDOWS
STUB        'WINSTUB.EXE'
CODE        PRELOAD MOVEABLE DISCARDABLE
DATA        PRELOAD MOVEABLE MULTIPLE
HEAPSIZE    1024
STACKSIZE   8192

sections.p: NAME is the module name Windows shows. EXETYPE WINDOWS marks a Windows program rather than a DOS one. STUB is a tiny DOS program that prints an error if someone runs the EXE from plain DOS. CODE and DATA say how segments load; MOVEABLE DISCARDABLE lets Windows throw code away and reload it from disk when RAM is tight. MULTIPLE data gives each running copy its own data segment — that is why hPrevInstance mattered in WinMain.
A DLL is also a module, but it uses LIBRARY instead of NAME, and it exports entry points. Other programs load it with LoadLibrary / GetProcAddress, or the linker binds the import at build time.

Declare the DLL function with the same calling convention the export used (FAR PASCAL on Win16), and either link an import library or load it by hand. Always match the ordinal or name you put under EXPORTS.

practice.q: What does a .DEF file tell the linker?
practice.why: NAME/LIBRARY, EXETYPE, CODE/DATA and EXPORTS are the usual contents.
options: Module name, type, segment flags and exports
The colour of the title bar
practice.answer: Module name, type, segment flags and exports

practice.q: Which .DEF keyword starts a DLL instead of an EXE?
practice.why: EXE modules use NAME; DLLs use LIBRARY.

practice.q: Why mark CODE as DISCARDABLE?
practice.why: On small RAM machines discardable code frees memory when another program needs it.
options: Windows can throw the segment away and reload it from disk
practice.answer: Windows can throw the segment away and reload it from disk

practice.q: What does DATA MULTIPLE mean for an EXE?
practice.why: That is why the first instance registers the class and later copies see a non-NULL hPrevInstance.
options: Each running copy gets its own data segment
Data is shared with every DLL
practice.answer: Each running copy gets its own data segment

practice.q: Where do you list AddNuts so other modules can call it?
practice.why: EXPORTS publishes the names or ordinals other modules may import.

practice.q: What should LibMain return on success?
practice.why: A zero return means the DLL failed to initialise and Windows unloads it.
